blocks: Ninety-Six Million Fake Calls.
Three months. Ninety-six million phone calls. The FCC says the callers faked their numbers, so they looked like they came from your own neighborhood.
Then a record fine. Then a Senate hearing, where the man behind the calls said, I am not the kingpin of robocalling that is alleged.
Then a brand new law. And yet, your phone still rings. Here is what really changed, and what did not.
Chapter one. The Call.
Your phone rings. The number looks local. It even starts with the same six digits as your own number.
That trick is called neighbor spoofing. The caller fakes the number on your screen, copying the first six digits of the number being called.
You pick up. A recording says you have been chosen for an exclusive travel offer, from a brand you know. Press one to claim it.
According to the FCC, the callers used the names TripAdvisor, Expedia, Marriott and Hilton. Those companies did not make the calls. Their names were used without permission.
If you pressed one, you were connected to a call center. There, operators sold vacation packages, usually with a timeshare sales presentation.
Those packages were for Mexico and the Caribbean. The operators had no connection to the brands whose names were used to get you on the line.
The FCC says the man behind the recordings was Adrian Abramovich, a businessman from Miami.
From October to December of twenty sixteen, the FCC counted ninety-six million, seven hundred fifty-eight thousand calls. That is more than a million calls a day.
And the harm did not stop with the people who answered. The real owners of those faked numbers began getting angry calls back.
A local number on your screen is not proof of where a call comes from. In this case, that was the whole trick.
Chapter two. The Fine.
One hundred twenty million dollars. That was the fine. In June twenty seventeen, the FCC proposed it against Adrian Abramovich and his two companies.
In May twenty eighteen, the FCC made it final. He and both companies were held responsible together, for the full amount.
FCC Chairman Ajit Pai called it the largest fine in the agency's history. It was also the first under the Truth in Caller ID Act.
Here is the odd part. The FCC did not count all ninety-six million calls. It sampled eighty thousand, about a thousand for each day.
It counted each sampled call at one thousand dollars, which is eighty million. Then it added forty million more. That makes one hundred twenty.
The FCC found that every one of those eighty thousand sampled calls used a spoofed number. The fine was built on that sample.
Abramovich argued that no one is harmed unless they answer and stay on the line for about five minutes.
The FCC ruled otherwise. Under the law, what matters is whether he intended to cause harm, not whether harm was proven for each call.
Commissioner Michael O'Rielly agreed in part and disagreed in part. He doubted there is harm when a consumer never hears the message.
One more thing. This was a civil fine from a federal agency. It was not a criminal verdict. Those are different things.
A record fine. And a lesson: one fine does not change how the phone network works.
Chapter three. The Hearing.
Abramovich said no to the Senate. In October twenty seventeen, the Commerce Committee wrote to him. In November, his lawyer declined. Then came a subpoena.
On April eighteenth, twenty eighteen, he testified. The hearing was titled Abusive Robocalls and How We Can Stop Them.
Abramovich claimed fewer than two percent of people called interacted with the message. Senator John Thune did the math: two percent of a hundred million is two million.
He answered some questions. On others he invoked the Fifth Amendment. That is his right, and it is not proof of anything.
Senator Richard Blumenthal asked the chairman to consider holding him in contempt after he invoked the Fifth. That was a request, not a ruling.
He also said, I am not the kingpin of robocalling that is alleged. The kingpin label came from others, and he denied it.
He also said the resorts were real, offering real vacation packages. The FCC found no evidence that the carrier or the clients knew about the spoofing.
Other witnesses gave the scale. Lois Greisman of the FTC reported more than seven million complaints about unwanted calls in fiscal year twenty seventeen.
Rosemary Harold, the FCC's enforcement chief, told senators that robocalls were the agency's largest source of complaints.
The hearing ended without a fix for your phone. But Senator Thune went on to co-write the law that came next, with Representative Frank Pallone.
Chapter four. The Law.
Nearly forty-eight billion robocalls in one year. That was twenty eighteen, according to YouMail, up more than half from the year before.
A law already existed. The Truth in Caller ID Act of twenty ten bans spoofing that is meant to defraud, cause harm, or get something of value.
But it worked after the fact, case by case. Abramovich's calls ended in December twenty sixteen. The fine became final in May twenty eighteen, about seventeen months later.
So Congress wrote a new one. The Pallone-Thune TRACED Act passed almost unanimously and was signed on December thirtieth, twenty nineteen.
First, bigger penalties. For an intentional violation, the FCC can add up to ten thousand dollars on top of the base fine.
Second, more time. For intentional violations, the FCC now has four years to act. For the base fine, the window is one year.
Third, and most important, caller authentication. The law gave the FCC eighteen months to require a system called STIR SHAKEN.
Think of it as a digital signature. The carrier that starts the call signs the number. The carrier that receives it checks the signature.
If the signature is missing or fake, the call can be flagged or blocked. The law also protects carriers that block, and bans charging you extra for it.
The law also created a group of federal agencies to study how to prosecute these cases criminally, and told the FCC to pass evidence to the Attorney General.
The old law punished a fake number after the damage was done. The new one tried to catch it before you answer.
Chapter five. Still Ringing.
Fifty-eight and a half billion robocalls in twenty nineteen. About fifty-two and a half billion in twenty twenty-five. Those are YouMail's estimates.
In between, the number fell to nearly forty-six billion in twenty twenty, the pandemic year. Then it climbed back above fifty billion.
It reached fifty-five billion in twenty twenty-three, then fifty-two point eight billion in twenty twenty-four. The law did not shrink the problem. It leveled off.
To be fair, no one can say how high those numbers would be without the law. And YouMail is a private company, so treat these as estimates.
What did the law fix? Carriers must now sign calls. The FCC has bigger penalties, a longer deadline, and a database where providers certify their robocall defenses.
The FCC has used that power. In twenty twenty-three, it removed fourteen providers from the database. In September twenty twenty-five, another was removed for a false certification.
The next big case was bigger. In twenty twenty-one, the FCC fined two Texas telemarketers two hundred twenty-five million dollars, for about one billion spoofed calls.
What still fails? Smaller carriers got more time to comply, and in December twenty twenty-one the FCC had to shorten some of those deadlines.
And technology moves. In February twenty twenty-four, the FCC ruled that AI-generated voices count as artificial voices under the old robocall law. A ruling, not a new law.
The law made the fake number harder to hide. It did not make your phone go quiet.
So who pays the bill? Start with people who never made a call at all: the owners of the numbers that were faked.
The FCC order says they received angry calls from strangers, over calls they never made.
Then the brands. In April twenty sixteen, TripAdvisor reported several consumer complaints to the FCC about calls using its name.
Then everyone who pressed one. By Thune's math, that could be about two million people. The FCC order does not give a total count of victims.
In the first three months of twenty eighteen alone, the FTC logged about one point four million complaints about unwanted calls. About nine hundred thousand were about robocalls.
Now, what can you do? First, remember this case. A local number on your screen proves nothing. Every call the FCC sampled was faked.
If a recording offers an exclusive deal you never asked for and says press one, do not press anything. Hang up.
Do not call the number back. It may belong to a stranger, just as those faked numbers belonged to real people.
Ask your phone carrier what call-blocking tools it offers. The TRACED Act says carriers cannot charge you extra for call authentication.
To report a robocall, go to donotcall dot gov. To report fraud, go to reportfraud dot ftc dot gov.
You can also file a complaint at consumercomplaints dot fcc dot gov. The FCC explains spoofing at fcc dot gov slash spoofing.
Three months. Ninety-six million calls. A record fine, a Senate hearing, and a brand new law. And yet your phone still rings.
But now you know what a local number is worth, what the law fixed, and what it did not. That is how you stay one step ahead.
